cards.front: What is the Linux equivalent of Windows Administrator?
cards.back: The root user. Has full control of the Linux OS.

cards.front: What is systemd in Linux?
cards.back: The service manager that starts, stops, and manages daemons (background services). The kernel starts systemd, and systemd starts everything else.

cards.front: What are daemons in Linux?
cards.back: Background services in Linux - equivalent to Windows services. Managed by systemd.

cards.front: What is stored in /etc/passwd?
cards.back: User account database. One line per user: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. The 'x' means the hashed password is in /etc/shadow.

cards.front: Why is /etc/shadow more secure than /etc/passwd?
cards.back: Shadow contains the actual password hashes but is restricted to root only. Passwd is world-readable but only shows 'x' in the password field.

cards.front: What does /etc/hosts do and how does it relate to DNS?
cards.back: Maps hostnames to IP addresses. Checked BEFORE DNS - entries here override DNS for those names.

cards.front: Where are DNS server addresses configured on Linux?
cards.back: /etc/resolv.conf. Contains one or more 'nameserver' lines with the DNS server IPs.

cards.front: What is /etc/fstab used for?
cards.back: File System Table - lists drives and partitions to mount at boot, their mount points, and filesystem types. If a drive is missing after boot, check fstab.

cards.front: Linux command to list directory contents with permissions and ownership?
cards.back: ls -la (or ls -l). Shows type, permissions, links, owner, group, size, date, name for each item.

cards.front: How do you rename a file in Linux?
cards.back: mv oldname newname. Linux has no separate rename command - move is used for both moving and renaming.

cards.front: Linux command to delete a directory and all its contents?
cards.back: rm -r directoryname. The -r flag (recursive) is required because rm alone only removes files.

cards.front: What do chmod octal values 7, 6, 5, and 4 mean?
cards.back: 7 = rwx (read+write+execute), 6 = rw- (read+write), 5 = r-x (read+execute), 4 = r-- (read only). 0 = no permissions.

cards.front: chmod 744 sets what permissions?
cards.back: Owner (user) = rwx (7), Group = r-- (4), Others = r-- (4). Owner can read, write, execute. Everyone else can only read.

cards.front: What does chmod a-w filename do?
cards.back: Removes write permission for ALL users (owner, group, and others). 'a' = all, '-' = remove, 'w' = write.

cards.front: Difference between sudo and su?
cards.back: sudo: runs a single command with elevated (root) privileges. su: switches the entire terminal session to the superuser. Best practice is to use sudo rather than su.

cards.front: Linux command to change file owner to user 'jack' and group to 'backup'?
cards.back: sudo chown jack:backup filename

cards.front: What does grep do and what is the basic syntax?
cards.back: Searches file contents for a text string. Syntax: grep "searchterm" filename. Outputs every matching line.

cards.front: Linux equivalent of Windows ipconfig?
cards.back: ip address (or ip addr). Shows IP, subnet, broadcast, MAC, and IPv6 for each network interface.

cards.front: How does Linux ping differ from Windows ping?
cards.back: Linux ping runs continuously until you press Ctrl+C. Windows ping stops after 4 packets by default.

cards.front: Linux equivalent of Windows nslookup?
cards.back: dig. Same function (DNS query) but with more detailed output. Syntax: dig hostname

cards.front: Linux equivalent of Windows tracert?
cards.back: traceroute (full name). Same TTL-hop mechanism. Windows: tracert. Linux/macOS: traceroute.

cards.front: What does curl do in Linux?
cards.back: Retrieves content from a URL from the command line. Returns raw HTML or data. Used for scripting and testing web servers.

cards.front: Linux command to view real-time process info (CPU/memory)?
cards.back: top. Shows all processes updating every second. Load average at top shows 1-, 5-, 15-minute averages. Press Q to quit.

cards.front: ps command: what is the difference between ps and ps -e?
cards.back: ps alone: shows only the current user's processes. ps -e: shows ALL processes on the system.

cards.front: Linux command to view disk space usage by filesystem (human readable)?
cards.back: df -h. Shows each mounted filesystem with size, used, available, and % used. -h = human-readable (GB/MB).

cards.front: Difference between df and du in Linux?
cards.back: df: how much free space is available on each filesystem. du: how much space specific directories/files are consuming. Use du -h to find what is filling a disk.

cards.front: Linux package manager for Ubuntu/Debian vs Red Hat/Fedora?
cards.back: Ubuntu/Debian: apt (sudo apt install packagename). Red Hat/Fedora: dnf (successor to YUM).

cards.front: What does the nano editor use to exit?
cards.back: Ctrl+X. It prompts to save if changes were made.

cards.front: Linux file system check utility (equivalent to Windows chkdsk)?
cards.back: fsck (file system check). Checks for logical errors. Typically runs at boot before the filesystem is mounted.
